Iceland has voted against resuming talks on joining the European Union 13 years after they were broken off.
Public broadcaster RUV reported that 52.8% of 225,031 voters rejected the government's proposal, while 47.2% had said yes. Some 12,600 votes separated them.

However, debate in this island nation of almost 400,000 people centred more on its fishing industry rather than security concerns.
With some 270,000 people eligible to vote, RUV reported the turnout of 82.5% was the highest in any election in Iceland since 2009.
Already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone, EU membership would bring Iceland into the customs union and eventually the euro.
Iceland began its application to join the EU in 2009 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system.
Its application was already well advanced when a eurosceptic government came to power in 2013 and put talks on hold. Fishing rights was the biggest obstacle then - as it remains today.
Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters feared they would cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds under the EU's common fisheries policy.

"This is a great day, we've been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote," KristrÃºn said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.
The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"
A Yes vote would not have been a final decision on joining the EU, but a move towards an accession agreement, which would then have to be approved by a second referendum.
Equally, the No vote does not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.
While economic issues dominated the referendum campaigns, security concerns also featured.
Iceland is a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.

corpus.title: Iceland rejects EU membership plan in referendum held under the shadow of Trump’s Greenland threats
corpus.signal_text:
Icelanders have voted to stay out of the European Union, broadcaster RUV reported on Sunday, rejecting a government push to reopen membership talks and siding with those who said Iceland’s fishing waters were too important to risk.
Some votes from one constituency are pending but these were not expected to change the outcome, RUV said.
A ‘no’ vote will disappoint Brussels, as some officials had cast the island nation of 40,000 as a low-risk case that could help ease scepticism toward EU enlargement and strategically strengthen the bloc when Arctic security is in focus.
The government has framed membership as a shield against trade wars and Arctic rivalry and presented the referendum as a “now or never” moment, with Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadóttir warning that a “no” would put the membership question aside.
The government is due to hold a press conference at 1 p.m. (1300 GMT).
Decades of membership debate
Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009 when a financial crisis hit the country’s small, exposed economy. A Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.
Geopolitical turmoil, including war in the Middle East and US import tariffs, has brought urgency to an issue Icelanders have debated on and off for decades.
“Yes” campaigners have said joining the bloc could help to lower interest rates and offer more security in a world unsettled by the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about annexing another Arctic island, Greenland.
“No” campaigners said EU membership would threaten the island’s sovereignty and fishing waters.
The referendum campaign has fueled debate about Iceland’s place in the world, Frostadóttir told reporters after casting her ballot in the capital on Saturday.
“This is a great day. We’ve been waiting for this for years to be able to have a vote,” Frostadóttir said, adding that her government would continue its work regardless of the outcome.
Interest rates and the cost of living
Debates inside Iceland have focused on interest rates, fishing rights and the cost of living rather than on security.
Iceland has grappled with high inflation and interest rates that have made mortgages expensive. Supporters of a “yes” vote have said EU membership, and possibly adopting the euro, could bring relief. Iceland’s central bank interest rate is 8%, compared with 2.25% at the European Central Bank.

corpus.title: Icelanders say no to restarting talks to join the EU
corpus.signal_text:
Iceland has voted against restarting accession talks with the European Union in a referendum held this weekend.
A tally of votes on Sunday morning, reported by Iceland’s national broadcaster, RÚV, showed that Icelanders rejected the government’s bid to resume negotiations with the bloc, with 52.8 percent voting against and 47.2 percent in favor — a difference of some 12,600 votes.
Turnout was high across the country of almost 400,000 people with 82.5 percent of eligible voters casting a ballot. While the “yes” vote was widely supported in the capital, Reykjavík, the “no” vote prevailed in rural areas.

corpus.title: Iceland votes against resuming EU accession talks
corpus.signal_text:
Iceland votes against resuming EU accession talks
Iceland has narrowly rejected the idea of resuming talks on joining the EU, public broadcaster RUV has reported. Previous negotiations were halted 13 years ago.
The referendum on Saturday saw a high turnout, with more than 225,000 people out of a population of just over 394,000 coming to the polls.
After the ballot count concluded on Sunday, RUV announced that 52.8% said ‘no’ to resuming accession talks, while 47.2% backed the idea.
The ballot asked voters just a single question: “Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?”
The country’s capital Reykjavik voted ‘Yes’, while people in rural areas were overwhelmingly against the EU path, underlining a split between the two parts of the country.
Russian presidential investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev has welcomed the outcome of the referendum, saying in a post on X that “Iceland knows how to play great football and how to reject the failing EU’s migrants, bureaucrats, and warmongering.”
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir promised to hold a referendum by 2027, but moved it to an earlier date due to geopolitical tensions, including US President Donald Trump’s threats to annex neighboring Greenland, which is an autonomous territory of Denmark.
In January, Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Iceland, Billy Long, suggested that country could become the “52nd state” of the US, with himself as governor. However, he later apologized and called it a joke.
Before the vote, Frostadottir’s allies portrayed the EU as additional protection for the country, while Euroskeptics argued that Brussels itself was becoming increasingly militarized and confrontational. Iceland is already a founding NATO member and maintains extensive military ties with Washington.

corpus.title: Iceland votes 'No' to resuming EU talks
corpus.signal_text:
In a vote held Saturday, 52.8 percent of Icelanders rejected the resumption of EU entry talks suspended 13 years ago, while 47.2 percent voted 'Yes', according to the official tally published by RUV, the public broadcaster.
The result will be a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues to facilitate Iceland's accession.
The result will also likely bury the EU question in Iceland until at least 2028.
The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.
Amid growing international tensions, Iceland's current government headed by Social Democratic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir wanted to sound out Icelanders on deepening their ties to the EU.
READ ALSO: As Iceland votes on the EU, which countries could be next to join?
The small North Atlantic island is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area and the free-movement Schengen zone -- ties which will remain unchanged.
Technically, the referendum result is non-binding but the government has vowed to respect it.
The government will hold a press conference on Sunday at 1:00 pm (1300 GMT) to present its plans.
'We will be fine'
Debates ahead of the vote had mainly revolved around domestic and economic issues, even if the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump's ambitions for neighbouring Greenland -- which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions -- featured in discussions.
The campaign had "lifted discussions about the EU, about Iceland's place in the world, about our general geopolitical situation and status, to a higher level", Frostadottir said on Saturday after she cast her ballot.
She was openly in favour of a 'Yes', but "we will be fine also if it's a 'No'," she said.
Frostadottir had vowed that if Iceland rejected the resumption of entry talks, the EU membership issue would not be put back on the political agenda during her mandate, which ends in 2028.
The government had also said that in the event of a 'No', it would leave to parliament the question of whether or not to formally withdraw the country's EU membership application.
Political analysts had said they did not expect the government to resign in the event of a 'No' victory. Made up of three parties with differing views on EU membership, it could emerge weakened by a rejection.
